comparator.name: Data Science and Artificial Intelligence
comparator.route: Introduction to Image and Video Processing elective and Year 3 project with electives
comparator.sourceNotes: The 2025–2026 regulations, Appendix 1 and Articles 3.15, 4.2 and 5.3, establish the illustrated route. Each of the first two years has twelve 4 EC courses and two 6 EC projects. Year 2 includes one Period 5 elective. Year 3 has six 4 EC electives, a 6 EC project, three 4 EC core courses and an 18 EC thesis. A student who passes each year on schedule meets project and examination progression requirements. The thesis requires at least 138 EC overall, including 60 EC from Year 1 and at least 40 EC from Year 2. The current programme overview corroborates the broad structure. The component list is specific to the published 2025–2026 regulations.
components: Introduction to Data Science and Artificial Intelligence (KEN1110, year 1 core course)
Objects in Programming (KEN1220, year 1 core course)
Data Structures and Algorithms (KEN1420, year 1 core course)
Principles of Data Science (KEN1435, year 1 core course)
Computational and Cognitive Neuroscience (KEN1210, year 1 core course)
Probability and Statistics (KEN2130, year 2 core course)
Simulation and Statistical Analysis (KEN2530, year 2 core course)
Human Computer Interaction & Affective Computing (KEN2410, year 2 core course)
Natural Language Processing (KEN2570, year 2 core course)
Philosophy & Artificial Intelligence (KEN2120, year 2 core course)
Introduction to Image and Video Processing (Year 2 elective)
Project 3-1 (KEN3300, year 3 semester 1 project for external customers)
The 18 EC thesis requires 138 EC overall, including 60 EC in Year 1 and at least 40 EC in Year 2.

routeSelection.route: Introduction to Image and Video Processing elective and Year 3 project with electives
routeSelection.basis: The general degree has two Year 2 elective options. Appendix 1 lists Introduction to Image and Video Processing first. The Year 3 in-programme elective and project route is the regular route in Article 3.15.

core: Programming and software: procedural and object-oriented programming, software engineering and databases, learned through project work
Algorithms and computational problem-solving: data structures and algorithms, graph theory and the algorithmic side of data science
Mathematical foundations: discrete mathematics, calculus, linear algebra, probability and statistics, numerical methods and mathematical modelling
Data science and machine learning: principles of data science, data analysis and machine learning for modelling, analysing and interpreting data
Reasoning, decision-making and intelligent systems: logic, search, planning, optimisation, operations research and intelligent agents
Applied and research practice: semester-long project work on real problems and a bachelor's thesis written as a research paper
adjacent: Cognition, language and human-centred intelligent systems: computational and cognitive neuroscience, human-computer interaction and affective computing, natural language processing, with the programme's courses on cognitive psychology

Philosophy of science and of artificial intelligence: Philosophy & Artificial Intelligence, taught from the philosophy of science and the philosophical issues raised by the pursuit of artificial intelligence

Medical applications of data science and artificial intelligence: medicine named by the programme as a substantive application area, with student projects in healthcare such as software that interprets ultrasound images
Robotics and autonomous systems: robotics presented as an application area for artificial intelligence, and the design of intelligent agents and systems
Logistics and planning: data science and artificial intelligence for planning and decision-making in logistics
questions: How can data and artificial intelligence be used to make better decisions and to solve real-world problems, for example in health?
How can computers learn from data, reason and act intelligently, and how does this relate to human cognition and intelligence?

trace: teaches ordinary and generalised least squares and instrumental variables, with Monte Carlo simulation, to answer questions of causality and prediction; it makes a specific complementary contribution as the causal-inference and prediction methodology needed to analyse health outcomes and risks

teaches research design, operationalization, experimental design and sampling together with descriptive and inferential statistics; it makes a specific complementary contribution to the study of experiments, observational data, bias and summary statistics that UM's Principles of Data Science treats

examines AI fairness and bias, privacy, responsibility, the moral status of AI systems and the philosophical and psychological questions about human-AI interaction; it makes a specific complementary contribution to the philosophical issues raised by AI that UM treats in Philosophy & Artificial Intelligence

teaches planning for AI systems in deterministic and non-deterministic environments with uncertainty, partial observability and optimisation under constraints; it directly implements the planning and decision-making under uncertainty strand of the core, treated by UM in Reasoning Techniques and Operations Research

covers logic, discrete mathematics, patterns and structures with applications to computer science and algorithm construction; it directly implements the discrete-mathematics and logic foundation of the core

covers uninformed and informed search, adversarial search, constraint satisfaction and convex, linear and non-linear optimisation by rational agents with laboratory work; it directly implements the search and optimisation methods of UM's Reasoning Techniques

teaches reinforcement-learning frameworks and algorithms and has students build agents with neural networks that learn by trial and error; it directly implements the behaviour-learning agents of UM's Intelligent Systems
introduces relational database theory, SQL, normalization and query processing; it directly implements the database content of the core

teaches software planning, requirements gathering, testing, quality assurance, maintenance and code review through projects in C++ and Haskell; it directly implements the software-engineering strand of the core
teaches algorithm design and analysis, data structures and experimental performance analysis with laboratory work; it directly implements the algorithms and data-structures strand of the core

studies modern algebraic algorithms and solution methods for optimisation problems with algorithmic thinking and mathematical modelling; it makes a specific complementary contribution to the algorithmic problem-solving and optimisation content that UM's core addresses in graph theory, algorithms and linear programming

teaches data cleaning, manipulation and visualisation, including spatial and text data, and ends with an own research project analysing data; it directly implements the data-science process of exploring and preparing data that UM's introductory data-science course and Data Analysis address

teaches linear regression, classification, resampling, shrinkage, tree-based methods, support vector machines and clustering on real data; it directly implements the machine-learning strand of the core

teaches camera and image models, feature detection and the processing, analysis and understanding of image data with programming; it makes a specific complementary contribution as a data-science application of machine learning to visual data, the territory of UM's image and video processing elective

builds neural networks from scratch and in TensorFlow, applies them to vision and text and studies large language models; it directly implements the deep-learning side of machine learning and the neural-language-model content that UM addresses in Natural Language Processing

treats kinematics, motion and manipulation of autonomous robots and the computational problems they raise; it makes a specific complementary contribution to intelligent agents acting in physical environments, which UM's Intelligent Systems treats with robots as an agent type

teaches structured and object-oriented programming in Python with testing and debugging, and elements of discrete mathematics and computational problem solving; it directly implements the programming foundation of the core, which UM teaches in Procedural Programming and Objects in Programming
teaches differentiation, integration, complex numbers and differential equations through projects; it directly implements the calculus foundation of the mathematical core
teaches matrices, vector spaces and linear transformations; it directly implements the linear-algebra foundation of the mathematical core and of machine learning

teaches numerical methods for root finding, differentiation and differential equations with attention to algorithm accuracy; it directly implements the numerical-methods strand of the mathematical core

extends calculus to several dimensions and differential equations with computer algebra software for data analysis; it makes a specific complementary contribution as the multivariable calculus underlying optimisation and neural-network training

characterises linear time-invariant systems through impulse and frequency response, convolution, Fourier representations and transfer functions; it directly implements the dynamical-systems side of mathematical modelling taught in UM's Mathematical Modelling
covers probability theory, discrete and continuous distributions, sampling, parameter estimation and simulation; it directly implements the probability-and-statistics foundation of the core

introduces central themes of Western philosophy on knowledge, consciousness and responsibility, their relation to computer science and psychology and the methods of philosophical argument; it makes a specific complementary contribution as the philosophical foundation for the philosophy-of-science and philosophy-of-AI content of the programme

examines virtue ethics, deontology and utilitarianism and practical ethics; it makes a specific complementary contribution as the ethical theory needed to analyse the moral questions raised by intelligent systems

asks whether the mind can be explained neurobiologically and whether artificial systems, including large language models, can be conscious; it directly implements the philosophical issues about replicating human consciousness and intelligence that UM treats in Philosophy & Artificial Intelligence

teaches how disease, risk and change in population health are studied and how evidence for public-health decisions is critically evaluated; it makes a specific complementary contribution as the epidemiological use of health data that medical data science applies

studies the structure of the human body in relation to function across body systems, with attention to surface anatomy and imaging; it makes a specific complementary contribution to the anatomical knowledge needed to interpret medical images, the application the programme illustrates with software that detects features in ultrasound images

relates normal physiology to pathophysiology in six organ systems and derives symptoms from failures of function using clinical cases; it makes a specific complementary contribution to understanding the disease processes about which medical AI makes predictions and decisions

explores the neural mechanisms of perception and action and how the brain guides goal-directed behaviour using methods from cognitive neuroscience; it directly implements the perception and action topics of the cognitive-neuroscience strand

deepens neurophysiology and experimental cognitive neuroscience and treats memory, attention, executive function, emotion, social cognition and decision making; it directly implements the learning, memory and decision topics of cognitive neuroscience, which UM includes among the cognitive models relevant to knowledge engineering

examines how people acquire, produce and understand language, with the neuroscience of language, experimental approaches and links to computer science; it makes a specific complementary contribution as the human counterpart of the computational language processing in UM's Natural Language Processing

introduces cells, molecules, genetic information and the organ systems that sustain living organisms, with an orientation to health and biomedical science; it makes a specific complementary contribution as the biological foundation of the medical applications that the programme names as an application area for data science and AI

introduces functional brain anatomy, neuronal communication and the psychological and neuroscientific study of perception, learning and behaviour; it makes a specific complementary contribution to the cognitive and biological psychology that UM teaches in Computational and Cognitive Neuroscience, without covering its modelling of cognition

covers the molecular, cellular and systems physiology of the adult human body and its organ systems; it makes a specific complementary contribution to the physiological knowledge that medical data and clinical measurements describe

teaches multivariate statistical models, regression, logistic regression, factor analysis and experimental methods; it makes a specific complementary contribution to the applied data analysis (multiple regression, classification and dimensionality reduction) of UM's Data Analysis

examines the bio-psycho-social approach to health and illness, research findings and interventions in medical settings; it makes a specific complementary contribution to the health outcomes and behavioural factors that medical data analysis addresses

teaches systematic reviews and meta-analysis, computing effect sizes and synthesising results of many studies with R for evidence-based policy and medicine; it directly implements the statistical synthesis of medical evidence in the medical-application direction
Studies Internet protocols, operating systems, concurrency and resource management. It supplies computing infrastructure for implementing and deploying data-driven systems.

alternatives.concept: Use programming, mathematics and statistics to build data models and intelligent systems. Develop software and study algorithms, machine learning, computer vision, and how agents search, plan and learn.

alternatives.label: Data Science and AI for Health

alternatives.label: Cognition, Language and Artificial Intelligence
alternatives.labelReason: Explore how people and machines perceive, use language, and make decisions. Combine cognitive neuroscience and philosophy of mind with programming, machine learning, reasoning and robotics.
alternatives.concept: Explore how people and machines perceive, use language, and make decisions. Combine cognitive neuroscience and philosophy of mind with programming, machine learning, reasoning and robotics.
progression: Brain and behaviour precedes psycholinguistics and advanced cognition. Programming and linear algebra precede robotics. Machine learning and decision-making precede deep learning and reinforcement learning.

selection.assessment: Three plans develop the main technical core, medical applications, and cognition, language and philosophy. Each pair differs by at least four courses and has a distinct academic progression. Robotics contributes manipulation and motion planning, but a separate robotics option would largely duplicate the cognition and AI spine without a sustained embedded-systems or control sequence. Planning and optimisation contribute to logistics, but the available courses do not sustain a distinct supply-chain, operations or simulation sequence. Mathematical coursework supports subject knowledge for teaching, but there is no corresponding school-based teaching and subject-didactics pathway.

blocks: Both introduce data analysis. UCR develops data preparation, visualisation and analysis in R. Maastricht also introduces intelligent agents and search.
Both teach control flow and functions. UCR uses Python and Maastricht uses Java.
UCR introduces object-oriented programming within its first programming course. Maastricht offers a separate course in Java.
Both develop requirements, design, testing and code review. UCR practises software development in C++ and Haskell.
Both develop discrete mathematical reasoning, logic and proof.
Both develop differentiation and integration. UCR also applies differential equations to modelling.
UCR covers logic within discrete mathematics. Maastricht offers a separate formal logic course.
Both cover systems of linear equations, matrices, vector spaces and linear transformations.
Both cover numerical methods for roots, integration and differential equations. UCR also studies interpolation and algorithm accuracy.
Both study dynamic models, including transfer functions and state-space representations. UCR focuses on linear signals and systems.
UCR introduces linear programming within optimisation. Maastricht devotes a course to linear programming.
Both study algorithms and data structures. UCR includes experimental analysis of algorithm performance.
UCR studies graph algorithms within algorithms and data structures. Maastricht has a separate graph theory course.
Both teach SQL and relational databases. UCR covers normalisation, authorisation and query processing.
UCR covers sampling, experiments and statistical inference. Maastricht uses data-science methods to study inference from observational and experimental data.
Both study distributions, estimation and statistical inference. UCR also uses computer algebra for simulation.
UCR uses simulation in probability and statistics. Maastricht has a dedicated course in simulation and analysis of its outputs.
Both fit statistical models to data. UCR approaches modelling through experimental research.
Both cover classification, regression and clustering. UCR evaluates model performance using practical data.
UCR uses neural networks for text classification and introduces large language models. Maastricht has a dedicated natural language processing course.
Both study image processing and computer vision. UCR builds a recognition pipeline and tests it on new images.
Reasoning, optimisation, decision-making and intelligent agents
Both develop search and constraint-solving techniques. UCR includes optimisation and search in adversarial settings.
Both address constrained decisions under uncertainty. Maastricht also covers dedicated operations research methods.
Both study intelligent agents. UCR develops agents that learn through trial and error. Maastricht also addresses agent architecture and cooperation.
Cognition, interaction, philosophy and ethics of AI
Both introduce biological and psychological foundations of cognition. Maastricht also studies computational models of cognition.
UCR studies perception and behaviour. Maastricht develops methods for human-computer interaction and affective computing.
Both examine philosophical questions about AI. UCR focuses on ethics, bias and responsibility.
Research, project work, thesis and open electives

notes.text: Maastricht has dedicated courses in graph theory, simulation, natural language processing, human-computer interaction and operations research. UCR covers related topics across algorithms, statistics, machine learning, cognition and decision-making courses.

Maastricht combines its courses with a sequence of semester-long projects and a required 18 EC thesis. UCR offers related coursework and an optional independent research opportunity outside the scheduled courses.

audience.programmeDescription: Maastricht’s Data Science and Artificial Intelligence bachelor combines mathematics, programming and machine learning with applied projects and an individual thesis.
audience.comparisonExplanation: The Maastricht example follows the published 2025–2026 regulations. It uses the image and video processing elective and the regular Year 3 project and elective route. Course choices may differ in later years. The UCR options emphasise technical AI, health, or cognition and language.
